title: The Epicureans
orientation: This chapter presents Epicurus and his school as a coherent, lifelong-fixed philosophy of pleasure aimed above all at freedom from fear -- especially fear of the gods and of death. Russell traces Epicurus's biography, his hedonist ethics (with its surprising preference for tranquil 'static' pleasure over active pleasure-seeking), his materialist physics (borrowed from Democritus but modified with the 'swerve' of atoms to preserve free will), and the poet Lucretius, who versified the doctrine two centuries later. The chapter matters because it shows one major Hellenistic answer to the problem set up in Chapter XXV: how to secure a good, untroubled life when public affairs offer no security at all.
historical_background: Epicurus (342/1-270 B.C.) was born to a poor Athenian colonist family on Samos, was displaced as a refugee when Athenian colonists were expelled from Samos in 322 B.C., studied briefly under a follower of Democritus, and founded his school (311 B.C.) first at Mitylene and Lampsacus before settling permanently in Athens (from 307 B.C.) in a house with a garden, from which his followers were called 'the philosophers of the Garden.' His chief surviving disciple in later times was the Roman poet Lucretius (99-55 B.C.), writing in the last, troubled years of the Roman Republic; the school survived, with declining vigor, for roughly six hundred years, before being generally supplanted by Neoplatonism among philosophers and by Christianity among ordinary people.
philosophical_problems: What is the good life, and is pleasure really the sole good?
Is there a meaningful difference between 'active' pleasure (satisfying a desire) and 'static' pleasure (the resulting untroubled equilibrium), and which should the wise person pursue?
Can materialism (the world as atoms and void) be reconciled with free will, given a fully deterministic physics?
Does fear of the gods and of death rest on false beliefs that philosophy can dispel?
Can a philosophy be sincerely and consistently egoistic (all pursue only their own pleasure) while also placing enormous value on friendship?

philosophers_discussed.name: Epicurus
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Founder of the school; held that pleasure is the sole good, but -- distinguishing 'dynamic' from 'static' pleasure -- concluded that the wise life aims at freedom from pain and disturbance (ataraxia) rather than active gratification; built a materialist physics (atoms plus an indeterminate 'swerve') designed above all to remove fear of the gods and of death; taught with dogmatic authority that his followers were not permitted to question.

philosophers_discussed.name: Democritus
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: The atomist philosopher whose physics (atoms and the void) Epicurus adopted as the foundation of his own system, while never publicly acknowledging the full extent of his debt.

philosophers_discussed.name: Nausiphanes
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: A follower of Democritus who taught the young Epicurus philosophy at Teos; Epicurus later expressed only contempt for him, mockingly calling him 'The Mollusc.'

philosophers_discussed.name: Lucretius
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Roman poet (99-55 B.C.) whose poem 'On the Nature of Things' versified Epicurus's philosophy two centuries later without adding theoretical innovation; presents Epicurus in language of religious veneration as the hero who defeated the tyranny of Religion, and, unlike Epicurus, allows that sexual intercourse is harmless if divorced from passion.

core_concepts.name: Pleasure as the sole good (Epicurean hedonism)
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Epicurus held that pleasure is simply what makes life good, and pain is what makes it bad -- nothing else (honour, wealth, virtue for its own sake) matters except as a means to pleasure or the avoidance of pain.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The ethical doctrine that pleasure is the beginning and end of the good life, and that virtue, justice, wisdom, and culture have value only insofar as they serve or are 'referred to' the pursuit of pleasure and the avoidance of pain.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It is the foundation of the entire Epicurean ethical and physical system, and, revived essentially unchanged, becomes the basis of modern utilitarianism via Bentham.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Formulated by Epicurus in Athens from 307 B.C. onward and fixed, according to Russell, 'once for all' by its founder, unlike the continually developing doctrine of Stoicism.
examples: Epicurus's statement that he cannot conceive the good if the pleasures of taste, love, hearing, and sight are withdrawn
'The beginning and root of all good is the pleasure of the stomach; even wisdom and culture must be referred to this'
objections: Ancient critics (especially Stoics such as Epictetus) accused Epicureanism of being 'swinish' and lacking moral exaltation
competing_positions: Stoic ethics (Ch. XXVIII), which makes virtue, not pleasure, the sole good
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Directly anticipates Jeremy Bentham's utilitarianism; Russell explicitly compares Epicurus to Bentham on both hedonism and inconsistency (both were kinder in practice than their egoistic theory strictly required).
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Leads Epicurus to advise withdrawal from public life, since political power invites envy and disturbs tranquility.

core_concepts.name: Dynamic versus static pleasure
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Epicurus distinguished the pleasure of actively satisfying a craving (like the enjoyment of eating when hungry) from the calmer pleasure of simply not being troubled by any craving at all (the quiet state after hunger is satisfied). He judged the second, calmer kind of pleasure better and safer to pursue.
core_concepts.precise_definition: 'Dynamic' (or active) pleasures are those attained through the process of satisfying a prior desire that was accompanied by pain; 'static' pleasures consist in a state of painless equilibrium that results simply from the absence of unsatisfied desire, requiring no painful stimulus beforehand.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: This distinction leads Epicurus to redefine the wise life's goal as absence of pain (aponia) and freedom from disturbance (ataraxia) rather than the pursuit of intense pleasurable experiences, making his 'hedonism' far more austere in practice than the word suggests.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Epicurus's own refinement of earlier hedonist doctrine (e.g. of the Cyrenaics, though not named in this chapter), distinguishing his position from theirs.
examples: Epicurus living contentedly on bread and water, calling this itself a thrilling bodily pleasure
His preference to be always in the state of 'having eaten moderately' rather than 'in that of voracious desire to eat'

core_concepts.name: Materialist physics with the atomic 'swerve'
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Like Democritus, Epicurus thought everything is made of tiny indivisible atoms moving through empty space. But unlike Democritus, who thought atomic motion was strictly determined by natural law, Epicurus proposed that atoms occasionally swerve slightly and unpredictably, which lets new combinations of atoms form and, crucially, preserves room for free will.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Epicurus's physical theory that the world consists of falling atoms and void; atoms, which fall downward in an absolute (not merely earth-directed) sense, occasionally undergo a slight, uncaused 'swerve' from their straight path, producing collisions and (Epicurus hoped) making room for undetermined human choice within an otherwise mechanistic universe.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It lets Epicurus be a thoroughgoing materialist about the physical world while still denying strict determinism, which he needed in order to attack the religious/astrological doctrine of Necessity as forcefully as he attacked belief in providential gods.
core_concepts.historical_origin: A modification of Democritus's atomism, motivated by Epicurus's wish to deny both religious Providence and rigid cosmic Necessity.
examples: Russell's comparison of the atomic swerve to Eddington's interpretation of the principle of quantum indeterminacy
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Adopted with fidelity by Lucretius two centuries later; noted by Russell as anticipating, in spirit, modern physical indeterminacy.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Designed specifically to undercut the religious conception of Necessity, which Russell notes was, in Greece, religious in origin.

core_concepts.name: Freedom from fear of the gods and of death
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Epicurus thought most human misery came from fear -- fear that the gods punish us, and fear of what happens after death. He argued both fears rest on false beliefs: the gods, if they exist, are blissfully indifferent to human affairs, and the soul, being made of material atoms, simply disperses at death and can feel nothing afterward, so death is 'nothing to us.'
core_concepts.precise_definition: Epicurus's core therapeutic goal: to remove the two chief sources of human anxiety by philosophical argument -- first, by holding that the gods, though real, do not interfere in or punish human affairs, and second, by holding that the soul is material and dissolves at death, so that the dead have no sensation and therefore cannot suffer.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: This is presented by Russell as the entire motivating purpose behind Epicurus's otherwise abstract physics: 'It was through the problem of avoiding fear that Epicurus was led into theoretical philosophy.'
core_concepts.historical_origin: Central and original to Epicurus's system from its founding.
examples: 'Death is nothing to us; for that which is dissolved is without sensation, and that which lacks sensation is nothing to us'
Epicurus's view that the gods are rational hedonists who, like his own ideal sage, abstain from the burdens of governing
competing_positions: Popular Greek and 'barbarian' religion, including belief in punishment after death, which Russell says was far more widespread among the general population than surviving elite literature (e.g. depictions on 'Grecian urns') would suggest
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Lucretius makes this the emotional center of his poem, treating Epicurus as a liberating hero who defeated the tyranny of Religion.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: A direct, sustained philosophical attack on popular religious belief, motivated by its psychological costs rather than by disinterested theology.

core_concepts.name: Epicurean friendship and its tension with egoistic hedonism
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Epicurus taught that everyone always acts only for their own pleasure, yet he also prized friendship enormously and clearly loved his friends and their children without any calculating self-interest -- a tension Russell says Epicurus himself did not fully resolve.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Epicurus regarded friendship as the safest of social pleasures and, per Cicero, held it must be cultivated because life without it is neither safe, fearless, nor pleasant; yet he also stated that 'all friendship is desirable in itself,' a claim in tension with his official theory that all human action is ultimately self-interested pleasure-seeking.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Illustrates, for Russell, a recurring pattern in ethical egoists (he draws the same comparison for Bentham): personal warmth and generosity that exceed what their own theory of human motivation would strictly predict or require.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Reflected throughout Epicurus's surviving letters, which show real affection for his community ('our holy body') and for the children of his deceased friend Metrodorus, whom he provided for in his will.
examples: Epicurus's dying letter asking his correspondent to look after Metrodorus's children
His warm, informal letters to children of community members
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell draws a direct parallel to Jeremy Bentham, 'constantly seduced by his own kindly and affectionate nature into admirable behaviour' beyond what his official hedonist theory required.

arguments.title: Argument that death is 'nothing to us'
premises: The soul is material, composed of fine atoms (like breath and heat) distributed throughout the body.
Sensation depends on the soul's atoms being connected to and functioning within a living body.
At death, the soul's atoms are dispersed and are no longer connected to a functioning body.
Whatever lacks sensation cannot experience anything, good or bad.
arguments.conclusion: 'That which is dissolved is without sensation, and that which lacks sensation is nothing to us' -- death, therefore, is not an evil to be feared, since once it occurs there is no one left to suffer it.
arguments.explanation: The argument is meant to dissolve the fear of death entirely by denying that there is any subject left to be harmed after death occurs; while one is alive, death is not present, and once death is present, one is not.
implications: Removes what Epicurus considered one of the two greatest sources of human fear (the other being fear of divine punishment).
Depends entirely on his prior materialist claim that the soul is composed of dispersible atoms rather than an immortal, immaterial substance.

arguments.title: Argument for the superiority of static over dynamic pleasure
premises: Dynamic pleasures depend on a prior state of unsatisfied desire, which is itself a form of pain.
Static pleasures (the equilibrium of a satisfied, undisturbed state) involve no such preceding pain and are not vulnerable to the frustration of desire.
A wise person prefers the more secure, less pain-dependent form of pleasure.
arguments.conclusion: The wise person should aim primarily at static pleasure (freedom from pain and disturbance) rather than at the intense but pain-dependent satisfactions of dynamic pleasure.
arguments.explanation: This reasoning is what leads Epicurus, despite being a hedonist, to a life of extreme material simplicity (bread, water, occasional cheese) -- since indulging in strong dynamic pleasures (rich food, sexual passion, ambition) invites more pain, in anticipation or aftermath, than the pleasure is worth.
implications: Explains Epicurus's advice to avoid public life, wealth, honour, and passionate sexual love, all treated as sources of restless, pain-laden dynamic desire rather than secure static contentment.

key_distinctions: Presence of pleasure vs. mere absence of pain (Epicurus increasingly treats these as effectively identical, with absence of pain as the truest pleasure)
The gods' real existence vs. their total indifference to human affairs (as opposed to popular belief in divine punishment/reward)
Materialism about the soul (atoms) vs. immortality of the soul (rejected by Epicurus)
Determinism (Democritus, and later the Stoics) vs. Epicurus's atomic 'swerve' preserving free will
connections_to_earlier_philosophers: Epicurus's physics is a direct, though publicly unacknowledged, inheritance from Democritus's atomism (he denied Leucippus was ever a real philosopher and disparaged his own teacher Nausiphanes). Russell also notes that Epicurus's view of justice as a matter of mutual non-aggression to avoid fear of retaliation resembles later Social Contract theory, without being drawn from any named predecessor in this chapter.
connections_to_later_philosophers: Lucretius (99-55 B.C.) transmits Epicurus's doctrine essentially unchanged into Latin poetry. Russell draws an explicit parallel between Epicurus and Jeremy Bentham (both hedonists whose personal kindness exceeded their theory's egoistic requirements), and notes that the French philosophes and Bentham's followers revived doctrines close to Epicurus's, in conscious opposition to Christianity, at the end of the eighteenth century.
political_social_context: Epicurus's advice to withdraw from public life -- because political power invites the envy and hostility of others and therefore disturbs tranquility -- is a direct philosophical response to the chronic instability of the Hellenistic world described in Chapter XXV. The chapter also situates Lucretius within the political turmoil of the last years of the Roman Republic, contemporaneous with Julius Caesar.
religion_science_culture_context: Epicurus's central project is an attack on popular religion (fear of divine punishment and of an afterlife of suffering), which Russell insists was much more deeply and widely felt among ordinary Greeks than surviving elite art and literature (which tends toward cheerful depictions, as on 'Grecian urns') would suggest; Russell explicitly invokes Jane Harrison's scholarship on Greek religion's more primitive, fear-inducing strata (e.g., Orphism) to support this claim.
russell_presentation: Russell presents Epicurus with considerable personal sympathy, taking pains to defend him against Stoic-originated scandal (e.g. about his mother, or about debauchery in the Garden) as unreliable, malicious gossip. He stresses the coherence and sincerity of Epicurus's system: it is a genuinely therapeutic philosophy, aimed entirely at securing tranquility by removing the two great sources of Hellenistic fear (the gods and death), and Russell credits Epicurus with real intellectual consistency in following hedonism to its most austere conclusions rather than its most self-indulgent ones. At the same time, Russell is critical of Epicurus's intellectual narrowness: contempt for predecessors, dogmatic insistence that followers not deviate from his teaching, indifference to mathematics and logic, and a lack of genuine curiosity about which of several possible naturalistic explanations of a phenomenon (e.g. lunar phases) is actually true, since for Epicurus any non-religious explanation serves the therapeutic purpose equally well. Russell judges this incuriosity to be why the Epicureans 'contributed practically nothing to natural knowledge' despite their materialism. He treats Lucretius's poem as the vehicle through which Epicureanism became known to the modern world, emphasizes the striking historical irony that professedly anti-religious, materialist doctrines are presented by Lucretius with quasi-religious fervor, and closes by tracing Epicureanism's decline (in favor of Stoicism, then Neoplatonism among philosophers, and Christianity among the masses) and its distant revival by Bentham and the French philosophes.
critical_context: Interpretive note: Russell's insistence, based on Cyril Bailey's scholarship, that scandalous stories about Epicurus's mother or his community's morals originated as hostile Stoic propaganda is itself a historiographical judgment rather than a settled fact; Diogenes Laertius, our main ancient source, mixes reliable material with legend, so any modern account (including Russell's) necessarily makes interpretive choices about which ancient testimony to trust.
key_takeaways: Epicurus held that pleasure is the sole good, but distinguished 'dynamic' (active) from 'static' (equilibrium) pleasure and concluded the wise life aims at static pleasure -- freedom from pain and disturbance -- rather than intense gratification.
Epicurus adopted Democritus's atomism but added the unpredictable atomic 'swerve' so that his fully materialist physics would still leave room for human free will.

The entire purpose of Epicurean physics, in Russell's reading, was therapeutic: to remove the two chief sources of human fear -- divine punishment and death -- by argument, not to pursue disinterested scientific truth.
Epicurus's famous argument that 'death is nothing to us' rests on his materialist claim that the soul disperses and loses sensation at death, so there is no subject left to suffer it.
Epicurus prized friendship intensely despite an official theory that all human motivation is self-interested pleasure-seeking -- a tension Russell compares directly to Jeremy Bentham.

Because any non-religious explanation of a natural phenomenon served Epicurus's therapeutic purpose equally well, his school showed little curiosity about which explanation was actually true, and contributed almost nothing to natural science.

Lucretius's poem 'On the Nature of Things' transmitted Epicurus's doctrine into Latin two centuries later essentially unchanged, presenting Epicurus with the fervor of a religious deliverer from the 'tyranny' of Religion.
study_notes:
The single idea to hold onto in this chapter is that Epicurus's hedonism, properly understood, is not indulgent but defensive and austere -- almost the opposite of the everyday meaning of 'epicurean.' Because dynamic pleasures carry the risk of frustration and the aftermath of pain, Epicurus systematically prefers the safer, calmer good of simply not being disturbed. This is why he can consistently recommend bread and water, avoidance of politics, avoidance of passionate love, and a small, tightly bonded community of friends: each of these choices minimizes exposure to painful disappointment while still permitting the 'static' pleasures of a settled, contented life.

Notice, too, how tightly Epicurus's physics serves his ethics. He is not doing physics for its own sake; the atomic swerve exists to preserve free will against determinism, and the doctrine that the soul is material and mortal exists to abolish fear of an afterlife. When Russell criticizes Epicurus's indifference to which particular scientific explanation of a phenomenon is actually correct, he is pointing to exactly this instrumental relationship between Epicurean physics and its therapeutic goal: once fear of divine intervention is removed, Epicurus has gotten everything out of physics that he wants from it.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The view that pleasure is the only truly good thing, and pain the only truly bad thing.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The ethical doctrine, foundational to Epicureanism, that pleasure is the beginning and end of the good life, with all other apparent goods (virtue, wisdom, justice) valued only instrumentally, as means to securing pleasure or avoiding pain.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: A calm, untroubled state with no unmet desires and no pain -- the goal of Epicurean life, rather than intense excitement or gratification.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The equilibrium state Epicurus identified as the safest and truest form of pleasure, arising from the absence of unsatisfied desire and pain, as opposed to 'dynamic' pleasure, which depends on and follows a preceding painful want.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Epicurus's idea that falling atoms occasionally veer very slightly off their straight path for no determined reason, which lets new combinations of matter form and leaves room for free will.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Epicurus's modification of Democritus's strictly deterministic atomism: an uncaused, indeterminate deviation ('swerve') in the otherwise uniform downward fall of atoms, introduced to permit collisions that generate the world and to preserve human free will against physical determinism.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The view that the soul is made of physical particles (like fine breath or heat) spread through the body, and simply disperses -- ending all feeling -- when the body dies.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Epicurus's doctrine that the soul consists of material atoms distributed through the body, responsible for sensation only while connected to a living body, and dispersing (with consequent loss of sensation, but not of the constituent atoms) at death.

questions.prompt: How does Russell characterize the reliability of Diogenes Laertius as the main ancient source for Epicurus's life, and why does this matter?
questions.answer: Russell notes two problems: Diogenes Laertius readily accepts legends of little historical value, and much of his account reports scandalous accusations made against Epicurus by hostile Stoics, without always making clear whether Diogenes endorses or merely repeats these claims. This matters because it means such 'facts' (e.g. about Epicurus's mother) are more reliable as evidence of Stoic hostility than as evidence about Epicurus himself.
questions.explanation: Russell explicitly separates 'facts about the Stoics' (their willingness to invent scandal) from 'facts about Epicurus.'

questions.prompt: What is the difference between 'dynamic' and 'static' pleasure in Epicurus's ethics, and which does he consider it wiser to pursue?
questions.answer: Dynamic pleasure is the pleasure of actively satisfying a prior desire that involved some pain (e.g. eating while hungry); static pleasure is the calm equilibrium that follows once the desire is satisfied, involving no antecedent pain. Epicurus holds it wiser to pursue static pleasure, since it is unalloyed and does not depend on pain as a stimulus.
questions.explanation: This distinction explains Epicurus's preference for a simple, contented life over one of intense but risky gratification.

questions.prompt: Reconstruct Epicurus's argument for the conclusion that 'death is nothing to us.'
questions.answer: Premise: the soul is material, composed of fine atoms distributed through the body. Premise: sensation requires the soul's atoms to be connected to a living, functioning body. Premise: at death the soul's atoms disperse and lose connection to the body. Conclusion: since what is dissolved has no sensation, and what has no sensation can experience nothing, death involves no experience of harm for the person who has died, and is therefore nothing to fear.
questions.explanation: The argument depends entirely on Epicurus's prior materialist and mortalist view of the soul.

questions.prompt: According to Epicurus, do the gods exist, and if so, what do they do?
questions.answer: Yes -- Epicurus believed the gods exist (he thought the widespread idea of gods across cultures needed explaining), but he held they are entirely indifferent to human affairs: perfectly happy, rational hedonists who, like his own ideal sage, avoid the burdens of governing or intervening in the world.
questions.explanation: This removes the fear of divine punishment or reward that Epicurus considered a major source of human anxiety.

questions.prompt: Contrast Epicurus's official theory that all human motivation is self-interested pleasure-seeking with his actual attitude and behaviour toward friends, as Russell describes it.
questions.answer: Officially, Epicurus held that friendship, like everything else, is cultivated because it serves one's own safety and pleasure. In practice, however, Russell shows Epicurus writing with deep, apparently disinterested affection to his community ('our holy body') and providing for the children of his dead friend Metrodorus in his will, and even stating 'all friendship is desirable in itself' -- in tension with strict egoistic hedonism.
questions.explanation: Russell compares this directly to Jeremy Bentham, another hedonist whose personal warmth exceeded his theory's requirements.

questions.prompt: Which Roman poet transmitted Epicurus's philosophy into Latin verse roughly two centuries after Epicurus's death, and in what tone does he present Epicurus?
questions.answer: Lucretius, in 'On the Nature of Things'; he presents Epicurus in language of religious veneration, as a hero who defied and defeated the tyranny of Religion.
questions.explanation: Russell finds it striking that a materialist, anti-religious doctrine is presented with such quasi-religious intensity.

questions.prompt: Why, according to Russell, did the Epicureans contribute almost nothing to natural science despite being thoroughgoing materialists?
questions.answer: Because Epicurus valued naturalistic explanations only instrumentally, as a way of ruling out divine intervention; when several possible naturalistic explanations of a phenomenon existed (his example is the phases of the moon), he considered it pointless 'idle curiosity' to determine which was actually true, since any of them served his therapeutic, anti-religious purpose equally well.
questions.explanation: This shows the purely instrumental relationship between Epicurean physics and Epicurean ethics.

quiz.prompt: What did Epicurus hold to be the sole good in life?
quiz.explanation: Epicurus's ethics is a form of hedonism: pleasure is 'the beginning and end of the blessed life.'
quiz.related_concept: Pleasure as the sole good (Epicurean hedonism)

quiz.prompt: Which kind of pleasure did Epicurus judge it wiser for the sage to pursue?
options: Dynamic pleasure, since intensity of feeling is what matters
Static pleasure, the equilibrium free of prior pain and disturbance
Only intellectual pleasures, never bodily ones
quiz.explanation: Static pleasure does not depend on a preceding painful desire and so is safer and more secure than dynamic pleasure.

quiz.prompt: Why did Epicurus introduce the atomic 'swerve' into his physics, departing from Democritus?
options: To explain the phases of the moon precisely
To account for the existence of the gods
To make room for free will within an otherwise mechanistic, atomist universe
To disprove the existence of empty space
quiz.explanation: Democritus's atomism was fully deterministic; Epicurus added an uncaused swerve to preserve free will.

quiz.prompt: What are the two chief sources of fear that Epicurus's philosophy is designed to remove?
options: Religion (fear of the gods) and fear of death
quiz.explanation: Russell states that avoiding fear -- specifically religious fear and the dread of death -- is what drove Epicurus into theoretical philosophy.
quiz.related_concept: Freedom from fear of the gods and of death

quiz.prompt: Epicurus denied that the gods exist at all.
quiz.explanation: Epicurus believed the gods exist (since the idea of gods needed some explanation) but held they are wholly indifferent to human affairs.
quiz.related_concept: Freedom from fear of the gods and of death

quiz.prompt: According to Russell, what tension exists between Epicurus's official ethical theory and his actual behaviour toward friends?
options: He preached friendship but had no real friends
His theory holds all action is self-interested pleasure-seeking, yet he showed and expressed disinterested affection and care for friends and their children
He believed friendship was evil but practiced it anyway
There is no tension; Epicurus was perfectly consistent
quiz.explanation: Russell compares this directly to Bentham: both hedonists were 'seduced' by their own kindly natures into behaviour exceeding what pure self-interest theory required.
quiz.related_concept: Epicurean friendship and its tension with egoistic hedonism

quiz.prompt: Epicurus's argument that 'that which is dissolved is without sensation, and that which lacks sensation is ____ to us' is meant to remove the fear of death.
quiz.explanation: This is Epicurus's direct statement of the conclusion of his argument against fearing death.
quiz.related_concept: Freedom from fear of the gods and of death

essay_prompts.prompt: Explain why Epicurus's hedonism leads him, apparently paradoxically, to recommend a life of bread, water, and withdrawal from public affairs rather than a life of active gratification. Use the dynamic/static pleasure distinction in your answer.
rubric: Accurately explains dynamic vs. static pleasure
Connects the distinction to Epicurus's specific practical recommendations (diet, politics, love)
Uses at least one direct textual detail or quotation

essay_prompts.prompt: Russell argues that Epicurus's physics was pursued purely as a means to a therapeutic, ethical end (removing fear) rather than for its own sake, and that this explains the Epicureans' scientific unproductiveness. Evaluate whether this is a fair criticism of a philosophy that never claimed science was intrinsically valuable.
rubric: Considers whether instrumental use of physics is inherently a flaw
Draws on specific chapter evidence (e.g. the lunar-phases example)
